prompt: What does `stopped: length` mean in the output of `guard cost`?

choices.text: The server cut the reply at `max_tokens`
choices.why: Right: the model had not finished.

choices.text: The model finished its answer normally
choices.why: That is `stop`.

choices.text: The prompt was longer than the model accepts
choices.why: The prompt was 48 tokens.

choices.text: The reply was refused by a filter
choices.why: No filter ran in `cost.py`.

prompt: Without a limit, how many tokens long was the model's reply?
Why does the lesson say the reply is where the money goes?
hint: Compare the two counts and the two prices.

choices.text: The provider charges only for replies
choices.why: It charges for both; the prompt was cheap here.

choices.text: The prompt is cached and costs nothing
choices.why: Nothing in the lab caches prompts.

choices.text: The reply was longer and each token dearer
choices.why: Right: 526 tokens at four times the price of the 48.

choices.text: Replies are counted twice by the server
choices.why: Each token is counted once.

prompt: A reply that should be JSON stops with `length`. What should the code do with it?
hint: Lesson 9 had a loop for this.

choices.text: Show it to the client, since most of it arrived
choices.why: A cut-off JSON object is not JSON.

choices.text: Close the brackets and parse what is there
choices.why: That invents the missing part.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` until every reply fits
choices.why: That removes the ceiling on cost.

choices.text: Treat it as a failure, and retry or hand it on
choices.why: Right: lesson 9's retry loop, then a person.

prompt: OWASP's name for `LLM10`, the failure this lesson is about: unbounded ___.
With the per-account budget, how many calls of the looping account were served?
hint: Its row in the last table.

prompt: With only the ceiling for the day, what did the five honest clients lose?

choices.text: Nothing, since the ceiling caught only the loop
choices.why: Each was served 13 of 20.

choices.text: Seven questions each, all after 14:26
choices.why: Right: one account's loop became everybody's outage.

choices.text: Their whole day, from the first call
choices.why: They were served until 14:26.

choices.text: The alert, which went to them by mistake
choices.why: The alert goes to Tarefa, not to clients.

prompt: Why did spending stop at R$ 20,03 rather than exactly at the ceiling?

choices.text: The check runs after the call that crosses it
choices.why: Right: a ceiling that must hold checks the estimated cost before.

choices.text: Prices change during the day
choices.why: The prices are fixed in the file.

choices.text: Three centavos are lost to rounding each call
choices.why: Money is kept in millionths of a cent and rounded once.

choices.text: The alert at 80% added its own cost
choices.why: An alert costs nothing in the replay.

prompt: Match each limit to what it stops, as the lesson's table puts it.
hint: One item on the right is stopped by none of them.

prompt: A partner sends every request through one API key, on behalf of 200 end users. What makes a per-account budget mean anything there?

choices.text: A higher ceiling for the day, sized for 200 users
choices.why: A ceiling still stops everybody together.

choices.text: A separate API key typed in by each end user
choices.why: The partner's integration holds one key; lesson 7 kept it that way.

choices.text: The end-user id of lesson 7 on every call
choices.why: Right: the budget is counted per end user, not per key.

choices.text: Counting the partner's requests per minute
choices.why: That limits bursts, not a day's spending per person.

prompt: With both limits on, which statements are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The looping account was cut after 33 calls
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Every other client was served in full
choices.why: Yes: 20 of 20 each.

choices.text: The day's ceiling was never approached
An alert fired at 14:20
choices.why: That was the run with the ceiling alone.

choices.text: The total stopped at R$ 20,03
choices.why: That too was the ceiling alone.

prompt: What should a looping integration receive when its daily budget is spent?
hint: Something a program can act on.

choices.text: A generic error, so that nothing is revealed to it
choices.why: A generic error makes it retry.

choices.text: No answer, until the budget resets
choices.why: Silence looks like a network failure and invites retries.

choices.text: A reply from a cheaper model, without any notice
choices.why: Degrading is a choice to announce, not to hide.

choices.text: A 'budget spent' error with its reset time
choices.why: Right: distinct, and with the time it ends.

prompt: Why is "something went wrong" a poor refusal for an integration whose budget is spent?
hint: What does a program do with an error it cannot read?

choices.text: It leaks the size of the budget
choices.why: It says nothing at all, which is the problem.

choices.text: It retries: the loop again
choices.why: Right: the retry is the loop again, costing nothing and fixing nothing.

choices.text: It is too long for a log line
choices.why: Length is not the issue.

choices.text: It breaks lesson 9's output schema
choices.why: The refusal is from Tarefa's API, not from the model.

prompt: Which steps between full service and none does the lesson list? Choose all that apply.
hint: Worse than full service, better than nothing.

choices.text: a cheaper model for the rest of the day
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: a shorter `max_tokens`
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: the help centre's own page where one matches
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: raising the ceiling without telling anyone
choices.why: That removes the limit rather than degrading service.

choices.text: switching off the per-account budget
choices.why: That would let the loop back in.

prompt: The 80% alert fires at 03:00 and is first read at 09:00, after the ceiling stopped the assistant at 04:10. What did the lesson say an alert needs that this one lacked?

choices.text: A person who receives it and knows what to look at
choices.why: Right: an alert nobody reads in time is a log line.

choices.text: A lower threshold, such as 50%
choices.why: An earlier alert read at 09:00 is still read at 09:00.

choices.text: A higher ceiling for the night
choices.why: That spends more before anybody looks.

choices.text: A copy sent to every client affected
choices.why: Clients need to be told in the chat; the alert is Tarefa's.

prompt: Put the four limits in order, from the narrowest to the widest.
hint: From one reply to the whole day.
items: a ceiling for the whole day

prompt: With the per-account budget, how many of the looping account's calls were refused?
The lesson says none of its limits is correct. What makes one defensible?

choices.text: Matching the numbers of the provider's own limits
choices.why: The provider's limits protect the provider.

choices.text: Choosing the largest value nobody complains about
choices.why: That is a limit set by the loudest client.

choices.text: A note on why, against what traffic, until when
choices.why: Right: so the next person knows what they trade.

choices.text: Changing it every week to follow traffic
choices.why: Without a note, nobody knows why it moved.
